Down by 1, Great Britain, the two-time defending European champs, went for a 2-point conversion with less than 2 minutes remaining, only to be denied when Emily Kemp’s left foot came down out of bounds after catching a pass at the back of the end zone.

Mexico was able to run out the clock thereafter.

“I’m so excited,” Mexico’s Angela Funes Fresan told Olympics.com. “The goal was always to bring home a medal and an Olympic spot, so I’m really happy.”

The Aug. 12-16 World Championships featured men’s and women’s 16-team fields (four groups of four teams each) with two Olympic berths at stake. The U.S. men and women were already assured of automatic bids as the host country.

Both Mexican teams emerged from group play with perfect 3-0 records to advance to the quarterfinals.

There, the women edged Spain 27-26 in dramatic fashion after coughing up a 20-6 lead to fall behind 26-20. For its part, the men easily handled Panama 33-19.

However, both stumbled in the semifinals.

Mexico’s women, ranked No. 1 in the world, were humbled by Canada 20-6, while the men came up just short against World No. 1 USA, 42-40.

Nevertheless, since the U.S. men’s and women’s teams each advanced to the finals, both Mexico squads knew that a victory in their respective third-place game would qualify them for the Los Angeles Games, where Flag Football will make its Olympics debut.

The women did so; the men did not, missing out in heartbreaking fashion.

Mexico’s men still have a chance to qualify for the Olympics via next year’s Flag Football Continental Championships.

With reports from Sports Illustrated, Conade, BBC, SportsNet and ESPN

World.title: CCE: Mexico’s streamlined investment process has spurred US $3.5B in new business
World.content:
Listen to this article

Measures announced by the federal government in May to facilitate investment in Mexico have been “successful,” according to José Medina Mora Icaza, president of the Business Coordinating Council (CCE), an umbrella organization that represents 14 private sector groups.

After a meeting on Friday with government-private sector liaison Altagracia Gómez and Mexico’s Ambassador to the United States Roberto Lazerri, the head of the CCE said that the measures have spurred investments totaling more than US $3.5 billion.

El Embajador @robertolazzeri y Altagracia Gómez #CADERR destacaron la importancia del rol del #CCE en el contexto de la revisión del #TMEC. Coincidieron con el Pdte. @JoseMedinaMora en la importancia de desarrollar proveeduría local para atraer cadenas de suministro a la región y… pic.twitter.com/LT9121UYb4 — Consejo Coordinador Empresarial CCE (@cceoficialmx) August 14, 2026

“Soon we’ll have an announcement because there is already more than $3.5 billion in investments authorized [by the federal government],” Medina Mora told reporters in Mexico City.

He didn’t reveal specific details about the planned investment projects, but said the money would come from Mexican and foreign investors.

Medina Mora’s remarks came around three months after the federal government announced a package of measures within the Plan Mexico framework to unlock and accelerate investments, especially large and strategic ones, by shortening authorization times, simplifying bureaucratic procedures and offering greater regulatory certainty.

“We are accelerating processes, simplifying mechanisms and strengthening legal certainty, because we know that economic development requires clear rules, mutual trust and shared responsibility,” President Claudia Sheinbaum said at an event in Mexico City on May 4.

In accordance with guidelines announced on that date, authorities have a maximum of 30 days to approve or deny strategic projects exceeding 2 billion pesos (US $117 million) within the electronic, pharmaceutical, aerospace, energy or technology industries. For other industries, authorities have a 90-day deadline to respond to proposals.

Medina Mora praises federal government

The CCE chief told reporters that Gómez, head of the government’s business advisory council, acts as a “communication bridge” between the private sector and the Sheinbaum administration.

Medina Mora also said that the federal government’s investment committee is very efficient.

“The investment committee has been very successful. It meets every week,” he said.

“The projects we’ve sent have been approved quickly,” Medina Mora said.

He added that Sheinbaum has “given priority” to the rapid approval of investment projects.

One of 13 goals of Plan Mexico is to reduce the average time between an investment announcement and the execution of a project from 2.6 years to 1 year. Among the other objectives of the ambitious economic initiative are for Mexico to become the 10th largest economy in the world by the end of Sheinbaum’s term in 2030, and to create 1.5 million jobs in Mexico’s specialized manufacturing industry and other “strategic sectors.”

Medina Mora noted that economic growth rebounded in the second quarter of 2026, after a sequential contraction in the first three months of the year. He also said that investment is picking up.

In the first quarter of 2026, Mexico received foreign direct investment totaling a record high of nearly $23.6 billion, an increase of 10.4% compared to the same period of last year.

CCE chief expresses support for fracking

Medina Mora said that the federal government’s openness to large-scale fracking represents an investment opportunity for the private sector.

His remarks came a week after a group of scientists that was tasked with assessing the viability of so-called “sustainable fracking” in Mexico essentially gave its green light to the ongoing evaluation of fracking potential in two basins in northern Mexico, although it recommended against the use of the gas and oil extraction technique in the resource-rich Tampico-Misantla basin.

Medina Mora said that fracking technology “has advanced” and today “takes into account environmental protection and remediation in such a way that there are no [adverse] side effects.”

He said that access to the energy resources that can be obtained via fracking will allow Mexico to have “competitive advantages as a country.” Mexico is currently heavily dependent on the United States for natural gas.

Sheinbaum also asserts that fracking can take place safely and without excessive water use via the employment of new technologies. She said on Aug. 6 that no final decision had been made on large-scale fracking, although it appears very likely that Mexico will move to use the controversial extraction technique in order to boost domestic production of natural gas.

With reports from La Jornada and Infobae

World.title: In latest show of security cooperation, Mexico and US sign drone agreement
World.content:
Mexico and the United States signed a defense agreement on new technologies last week, further strengthening cooperation between the two countries on security matters.

U.S. Ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson on Sunday underscored the bilateral cooperation within the declaration of intent that will allow Mexico’s Defense Ministry (Defensa) to acquire drones and counter-unmanned aircraft systems.

Celebrating the agreement and the bilateral commitment to fighting organized crime, Johnson published an image of himself shaking hands with Mexican Security Minister Omar García Harfuch as his Photo of the Week.

“Under the leadership of President Donald Trump and President Claudia Sheinbaum, our cooperation continues to yield results,” he said.

The signatories of the non-binding declaration of intent were García Harfuch, General Héctor Ávila Alcocer and U.S. Army Secretary Daniel Patrick Driscoll. Afterward, Sedena confirmed that no models, quantities, cost or delivery dates have been agreed, and there is no purchase commitment.

In a separate social media post, Johnson said the pact strengthens strategic and operational capabilities, specifically by allowing Mexico’s Defense Ministry “to access the U.S. Army’s digital marketplace to acquire unmanned aerial systems and counter-unmanned aerial systems at competitive costs.”

The agreement follows a December meeting of the U.S.-Mexico Security Implementation Group during which the neighboring countries consented to expand cooperation in dealing with the increased use of drones by criminal organizations.

Also discussed at the meeting was security in the avocado-growing region of Michoacán, where residents have frequently complained about extortion and violence by organized crime cartels.

The situation in that western state prompted the U.S. government to momentarily suspend the avocado trade earlier this month.

With reports from La Jornada, El Financiero and The Rio Times

World.title: MND Local: What to know about crocodile, human encounters in Puerto Vallarta
World.content:
Last week, MND’s news desk reported on the growing number of encounters between people and crocodiles in Puerto Vallarta, including the deaths of 11 American crocodiles (Crocodylus acutus) across the region in recent weeks.

The number is disturbing. So, too, is the timing. Puerto Vallarta is in the middle of a rather active rainy season. Rivers are swelling, estuaries are filling and waterways that are normally separated from one another have become connected.

But there’s another part of the story that’s worth looking at more closely.

According to Jalisco’s Ministry of Environment and Territorial Development (SEMADET), the increase in crocodile sightings isn’t evidence that Puerto Vallarta suddenly has too many crocodiles. It’s largely about what the animals are doing, and where the water is taking them.

SEMADET says monitoring in the Bahía de Banderas region estimates a population of 300 to 350 crocodiles, at different stages of development. That figure covers the wider bay area, which straddles Jalisco and Nayarit, rather than Puerto Vallarta alone.

The agency specifically notes that the recent increase in encounters isn’t the result of overpopulation. That matters because it changes how we should view what’s happening.

During the rainy season, crocodiles naturally move between rivers, estuaries and the bay. Heavy rainfall and increased water flow can carry them into areas they may not normally occupy, including closer to beaches and places where people live, work and play.

In other words, a crocodile appearing somewhere unexpected doesn’t necessarily mean there are more crocodiles. It also means that the boundaries between their usual habitats have temporarily changed. And that’s where things get complicated for a city like Puerto Vallarta.

Development on crocodile habitat in Puerto Vallarta

We’ve built homes, hotels, roads and businesses around the same waterways that crocodiles have used for generations. The animals haven’t suddenly moved into our neighborhoods. In many cases, we’ve expanded into theirs.

That doesn’t mean people should accept dangerous encounters or take unnecessary risks. A crocodile is a wild predator, and the fatal attack on a 28-year-old Mexico City visitor in June was a sobering reminder that these animals can pose a very real threat.

But SEMADET’s message is that protecting people and protecting crocodiles aren’t mutually exclusive goals. The agency is calling for coexistence, not the removal or killing of animals simply because they’ve appeared where people can see them.

SEMADET LLAMA A PROTEGER FAUNA SILVESTRE TRAS MUERTE DE 11 COCODRILOS EN PUERTO VALLARTA La Secretaría de Medio Ambiente y Desarrollo Territorial @SemadetJal hizo un llamado a respetar la fauna silvestre de la región de Puerto Vallarta y Bahía de Banderas, luego de que en las… — Jalisco Noticias (@notijaliscotv_) August 15, 2026

The American crocodile is protected under Mexico’s environmental regulations because of its role in the ecosystems associated with rivers, wetlands, estuaries and coastal areas. SEMADET has explicitly condemned acts of aggression towards the animals and says coordinated efforts are being strengthened to address both conservation and public safety.

That’s particularly significant following the deaths of the 11 adult crocodiles reported in the region. While authorities are investigating the circumstances surrounding those deaths, the agency’s position is clear. Encounters with wildlife aren’t a license to kill them. The response, instead, is supposed to be prevention.

Response to crocodile attacks

SEMADET says it is working with federal, state and municipal authorities, academics and conservation organizations through the Mesa de Trabajo Humano–Cocodril (Human-Crocodile Working Group), a longstanding interagency effort focused on improving coexistence between people and crocodiles in the region. Plans include improving and standardizing warning signs in areas where interactions are more likely, particularly river mouths, as well as strengthening monitoring and public education.

The city has also increased surveillance in areas where crocodiles are more likely to appear, while warning flags and other measures are being used to alert residents and visitors.

For those of us who live here, perhaps the most useful part of SEMADET’s message is also the simplest. During the rainy season, assume that waterways can change.

A river that looks familiar in February may be a very different environment after days of heavy rain in August. An estuary can connect with the ocean, floodwaters can move wildlife, and a crocodile that normally stays well away from people can suddenly find itself somewhere neither it nor we expected, or want, it to be.

If you see one, the advice is not to approach it, feed it, throw things at it or try to chase it away. SEMADET recommends increasing your distance immediately and moving away calmly. If the animal approaches or behaves aggressively, move quickly away from the water in a straight line.

New app for crocodile sightings

Sightings should be reported to 911, particularly if the animal is near people or in an area where an encounter is likely. SEMADET’s Puerto Vallarta regional office can also be contacted at 33 3030 8250 for environmental information and follow-up.

The Jalisco Alerta app, available on both the Apple and Google Play stores, is a state emergency and public-safety platform that provides alerts and information about incidents and potential risks. It is currently being expanded to provide real-time information about crocodile sightings in Puerto Vallarta.

According to Jalisco Civil Protection, information within the app will be updated using reports from residents, Civil Protection monitoring and known crocodile locations. The app will allow users to see areas where crocodiles have recently been reported, giving residents and visitors another way to stay informed and avoid potential encounters.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Jalisco Alerta (@jalisco.alerta)

None of this information makes seeing a crocodile on a beach any less startling. But it does give us a better understanding of why it’s happening. Puerto Vallarta’s rainy season crocodile encounters aren’t simply a story about animals becoming a nuisance. They’re a reminder that this is still a place where rivers, wetlands, mangroves and the ocean are part of a living ecosystem, even as the city around them continues to grow.

The answer, according to SEMADET, isn’t to eliminate the animals because they’re inconvenient or frightening. It’s to better understand where they are, why they’re moving and how people can avoid encounters in the first place.

Learning to live alongside wildlife doesn’t mean ignoring the risk. It means understanding it.

World.title: US returns 3 fugitives to face charges in Mexico
World.content:
U.S. Ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson said Sunday that U.S. authorities had returned to Mexico three fugitives wanted for crimes including murder.

In a social media post, Johnson wrote that one of the fugitives is a member of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG), one of eight Mexican criminal groups that the U.S. government has designated as foreign terrorist organizations.

Our cooperation, driven by @POTUS @realDonaldTrump and President @ClaudiaShein, sends criminals a clear message: you will be caught and held accountable. In just one day, U.S. authorities returned three fugitives wanted in Mexico: a member of the CJNG narco-terrorist… pic.twitter.com/DpRj0jxvsd — Embajador Ronald Johnson (@USAmbMex) August 16, 2026

“Our cooperation, driven by @POTUS @realDonaldTrump and President @ClaudiaShein, sends criminals a clear message: you will be caught and held accountable,” he wrote on X.

“In just one day, U.S. authorities returned three fugitives wanted in Mexico: a member of the CJNG narco-terrorist organization wanted on a firearms charge in Guanajuato, a fugitive wanted for murder in Zacatecas, and a third wanted for fraud,” Johnson wrote.

Photographs included in the ambassador’s post showed the fugitives in the custody of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Johnson didn’t say where or when the suspects were detained and handed over to Mexican authorities, and he didn’t identify them by name.

His announcement on Sunday came two months after he said on X that the United States had transferred 313 wanted criminals to Mexico to face justice during President Donald Trump’s second administration. Johnson’s June 15 social media post came almost a month after the Mexican government asserted that the United States hadn’t sent to Mexico any of the 269 people whose extradition it requested between January 2018 and May 2026.

“They haven’t sent anyone,” President Claudia Sheinbaum said on May 19.

She said those people include factureros (fake invoice brokers), ex-governors, people accused of organized crime and people linked to the disappearance of 43 students in Guerrero in 2014.

“There has been no handover of any of these alleged criminals to Mexico,” Sheinbaum said, although in 2022 former Chihuahua governor César Duarte was extradited to Mexico from the U.S. to face corruption charges.

“What does Mexico always ask for? … Reciprocity. Why haven’t they handed anyone over?” asked the president, whose government has sent over 90 organized crime figures to the U.S. in three large transfers that took place in January 2026, August 2025 and February 2025.

U.S. authorities are currently seeking the extradition of Sinaloa Governor Ruben Rocha Moya and other current and former Sinaloa-based officials who U.S. prosecutors accuse of drug trafficking in league with the Sinaloa Cartel. Sheinbaum has endorsed the determination from the FGR and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs that the U.S. Justice Department hasn’t provided sufficient “proof” to establish the probable guilt of Rocha, who is currently on leave, and the other defendants, two of whom turned themselves in to U.S. authorities in May.

With reports from El Financiero

World.title: Opinion: Does it feel safe to go to school in the United States after growing up in Mexico?
World.content:
My first article explored my transition from Mexican schools to American ones.

Today, I want to address the question I am asked most often, having been raised and schooled in Mexico: Is it safe for students to attend school here?

“Attention, this is a lockdown drill. Please remain in your classrooms and lock the doors.” For many students across the United States, these words have become an all-too-familiar refrain.

At my high school in California, lockdown drills are an annoyingly regular part of life, prompted by the grim reality of school shootings. In 2025, the K-12 School Shooting Database Omnilert recorded 233 school shooting incidents, although totals vary significantly depending on how a “school shooting” is defined.

It wasn’t until I moved to California that lockdown drills became a part of my school experience. In Mexico, where I attended school until I was 15, school shootings are practically unheard of. I still remember my first drill, two weeks into sophomore year. I was in English class when an unfamiliar voice blared over the speakers, telling us to turn off the lights, lock the doors and sit silently in the back of the classroom. Confusion was written all over my face, but not because of the drill. When I looked around, everyone else seemed completely unfazed, having seemingly done this hundreds of times before.

After that, I started to notice just how normal it all was. School shootings were mentioned in assemblies, safety procedures were constantly reviewed and we had around five more lockdown drills just that year. Everyone seemed to understand the seriousness of the issue after hearing about it constantly throughout their young lives.

Ironically, when I tell my American friends I grew up in Mexico, their first question is almost always about safety.

Yes, cartels and corruption do exist in Mexico. But no, I have never witnessed a murder, been threatened or traveled to school in a bulletproof car. As a student growing up in San Miguel de Allende, I never faced that kind of danger.

What sets the United States apart (and makes questions about safety in Mexico feel so ironic) is that school shootings are not a predictable kind of danger. They are random, devastating and disturbingly common acts of violence that can shatter the lives of innocent people because of the actions of a single individual.

As a student who attended private, not public, schools in both Mexico and the United States, I recognize that my experience is not the norm. Even so, comparing two similarly resourced educational environments has allowed me to notice clear differences in how school safety is experienced in each country.

My schools here in Mexico were overly cautious, if anything. The bilingual school I attended from fourth through ninth grade, Colegio Newland, had guard dogs protecting the grounds at night and a QR code system for students and adults entering campus each day. I never once felt my safety was threatened at school.

And this focus on safety isn’t limited to the private schools I attended. The Guanajuato Education Ministry provides both public and private schools with protocols for emergencies ranging from evacuations and violence to armed individuals and shootings. Schools are also encouraged to assess risks, create safety plans and regularly practice how to respond.

By contrast, my California boarding school has security guards and locks its front gates at night, but it lacks the advanced measures I grew accustomed to in Mexico. Last year, our classes were even canceled for a day because a neighboring school received a bomb threat. Even so, lockdown drills are routine.

When I lived in Mexico, my friends and I spent most afternoons in the center of San Miguel, getting esquites, papas preparadas, even Starbucks. We stayed out late and would walk home together, yet I never felt unsafe. I used to think that was because I always had my twin brother around, but after moving to the United States, I realized he wasn’t scaring anyone away.

In California, my friends and I spent many weekends in San Francisco. Once, while riding a bus near the Financial District, a fight broke out and quickly became violent. It felt like I was rewatching Fight Club, except there was no Brad Pitt. The people involved kept running on and off the bus, screaming at each other. My friends and I, all international students, watched in horror. But when I looked around, my confusion came back because I noticed the same thing had happened again: everyone else appeared completely unfazed.

Danger should never feel normal, yet the nonchalance of my classmates and the people on that bus made me realize just how normalized it can become after frequent exposure.

Now, that’s not to say San Francisco is unsafe and Mexican cities aren’t. But I’ve spent plenty of time in Mexico City, a huge city with a rough reputation in some places, and the worst violence I’ve experienced was a man winking at me on the street.

Nonetheless, it is important to acknowledge that my experience is not representative of every part of Mexico. The country faces very real security challenges, and many communities experience them far more directly than I ever did.

Mexico is my home, and hearing people automatically associate it with danger is beyond frustrating. Not just because I love the country and its people, but because it isn’t the Mexico I know. My experience isn’t everyone’s, but it has shown me how easily stereotypes can shape the way people see a place they’ve never lived in or even been to. That’s why, whenever someone assumes Mexico is too dangerous to raise a family or attend school, I feel the need to tell them about the home I know instead.

Zella Golden grew up in San Miguel de Allende and is a senior in high school in Marin, California. Golden is completing an internship with MND.

World.title: CDMX declares pan dulce a piece of Intangible Cultural Heritage
World.content:
Mexican pan dulce (sweet bread) has officially been declared Intangible Cultural Heritage of Mexico City, a recognition aimed at safeguarding one of the country’s most fundamental culinary traditions.

The initiative was driven jointly by the city’s Ministry of Culture and the National Chamber of the Baking, Pastry and Related Industries (Canainppa), a trade organization with more than 80 years of history representing Mexico’s bread industry. Beyond advocacy, the chamber provides its members with legal, tax and operational guidance, along with specialized training, as part of its broader mission to strengthen artisanal baking and support the growth of bakery businesses nationwide.

The declaration was approved during the First Extraordinary Session 2026 of Mexico City’s Interinstitutional Commission on Cultural, Natural and Biocultural Heritage. The next step is formal publication in the city’s Official Gazette, expected in September.

According to Julián Castañón Fernández, president of the Canainppa, the declaration is “not merely a technical document. It is a living testament to our traditions, to the creativity of our master bakers and to the cultural scene of Mexico City and Mexico as seen by the world,” he said during the Aug. 7 Session.

Canainppa also submitted a request to the city’s Heritage Commission for pan dulce to be recognized as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity by UNESCO. That proposal was approved and now moves forward, with backers arguing the tradition goes far beyond food — it’s woven into collective memory, celebrations and everyday customs across Mexican communities.

From conchas to orejas, sweet bread has long been a fixture of Mexican mornings and family gatherings — recently motivating an internet campaign defending its greatness in response to foreign haters.

With reports from Aristegui Noticias and El Financiero

World.content:

The fire happened at the Tolosa substation, on calle 528 between Camino General Belgrano and calle 9. Why The cause is still under investigation, and no official reason has been confirmed yet.

A fire at a key substation left thousands without electricity in La Plata. Restoration is ongoing, but no customer count has been published.

A fire at Edelap’s Tolosa substation cut power to thousands of users in La Plata early on Monday, August 17. The cause remains under investigation.

Fire at the Tolosa substation leaves thousands in the dark

A fire started at Edelap’s Tolosa substation at 02:30 on Monday. The substation is on calle 528 between Camino General Belgrano and calle 9.

The fire cut power for thousands of users in La Plata. The cause is still being looked into, and Edelap has not given a customer number.

Firefighters, Defensa Civil, and Edelap workers came to the scene. Traffic lights stopped working in the affected areas, which caused traffic problems.

By mid-morning, the fire was under control. Work to fix the power supply went on for the rest of the day.

Affected neighborhoods and the size of the outage

The blackout hit several neighborhoods in La Plata. These included the town centre, Tolosa, Ringuelet, Villa Castells, San Carlos, José Hernández, and Gonnet.

It was not clear how many people lost power. Edelap only said ‘thousands’ were affected, with no exact number.

The confirmed number of users who lost supply is not available.

Edelap’s response and restoration efforts

Edelap led the effort to restore power. The company said the fire was controlled and restoration was happening, but it gave no customer count.

Edelap did not say what caused the fire. It was still being investigated when the reports were made.

People in the affected areas were told to stay away from the substation. Emergency crews kept working all day.

What is confirmed and what is still under investigation

A fire at the Tolosa substation on August 17 caused a power cut. The fire began at 02:30 and was controlled by mid-morning.

The outage hit La Plata town centre, Tolosa, Ringuelet, Villa Castells, San Carlos, José Hernández, and Gonnet. Traffic lights stopped working.

The exact cause of the fire is still unknown. No official cause has been given, and Edelap has not released a customer number.

Also not confirmed: any specific number of affected users.

Political response and regulatory questions

Senator Marcelo Leguizamon, from the Hechos group in the Buenos Aires provincial Senate, has asked for official information about the fire. He wants a special committee to look into it.

He also wants the head of OCEBA, the provincial energy regulator, to be questioned. He has asked for a review of Edelap’s contract.

No regulatory penalty has been issued yet. The political response shows worries about how the situation was handled and how reliable the power grid is.

Why this matters for Latin American readers

If you live in a big Latin American city, you know one failure can leave whole areas dark. This La Plata blackout shows the same problem: one substation fire, and many homes lose power for hours.

For investors in Edelap or its parent companies, this is a reminder of operational risks. Regulators may look into the matter, and people could ask for compensation, but no exact amounts were given.

The blackout also shows why the power grid needs more investment. Old equipment and higher demand mean similar failures can happen in other places in the region.

For local people, it is a useful warning: save your emergency numbers, keep flashlights close, and check on neighbors who use electric medical devices. The grid is getting better, but it is not unbreakable.

What the province is being asked to do

The political response arrived before any official finding. Marcelo Leguizamon, a senator for the Hechos bloc in the Buenos Aires provincial senate, has filed formal requests for information.

He wants a bicameral commission set up to look at what happened. He has also asked for the head of OCEBA, the provincial electricity regulator, to be questioned by legislators.

His fourth demand goes further — a review of Edelap’s concession itself. That is the licence under which the company distributes power in the region.

No regulator has issued a sanction. The cause of the fire is still being investigated, so any finding of responsibility is some way off.

Where the power went out

The outage reached the centre of La Plata and the neighbourhoods around it. Tolosa, Ringuelet, Villa Castells, San Carlos, Jose Hernandez and Gonnet all lost supply.

Traffic lights failed across the affected area, which made driving difficult during the morning. Firefighters, Defensa Civil and Edelap crews worked at the site.

Frequently Asked Questions

Edelap has not published a count. Reports say ’thousands’ were affected. When was power restored? The fire was brought under control by mid-morning. Restoration continued through the day. Which areas were affected? La Plata town centre, Tolosa, Ringuelet, Villa Castells, San Carlos, José Hernández, and Gonnet. What is the political response? Senator Marcelo Leguizamon filed requests for information and wants a bicameral commission, OCEBA’s president questioned, and Edelap’s concession reviewed.

World.content:
Peru · Public Finance

Key Facts The clash Peru’s finance minister, Elmer Cuba, says a law raising retired teachers’ pensions breaks the Constitution. The government is taking it to the Constitutional Court.

Peru’s finance minister, Elmer Cuba, says a law raising retired teachers’ pensions breaks the Constitution. The government is taking it to the Constitutional Court. Pension law Ley No. 32581, called the ‘Ley de pensión digna’, sets retired teachers’ pensions at S/3,500.70, which is about US$1,041.

Ley No. 32581, called the ‘Ley de pensión digna’, sets retired teachers’ pensions at S/3,500.70, which is about US$1,041. Cost The Consejo Fiscal, which is the independent fiscal watchdog, says the cost is at least S/8,000 million a year, or about US$2,378 million.

The Consejo Fiscal, which is the independent fiscal watchdog, says the cost is at least S/8,000 million a year, or about US$2,378 million. Legal basis Cuba argues Congress does not have the ‘iniciativa de gasto’, which means spending initiative. That power belongs to the Executive.

Cuba argues Congress does not have the ‘iniciativa de gasto’, which means spending initiative. That power belongs to the Executive. Actions The government is taking the law to the Tribunal Constitucional. The Colegio de Economistas is doing the same, but separately.

The government is taking the law to the Tribunal Constitucional. The Colegio de Economistas is doing the same, but separately. Congress raise Workers at Congress got a 15% pay rise through a collective agreement. Fernando Rospigliosi, then president of Congress, signed it.

Elmer Cuba says Congress overstepped its powers with a S/3,500.70 (about US$1,040) pension law and plans a court challenge.

Peru’s Economy and Finance Minister Elmer Cuba has called a teacher pension law illegal. He says Congress violated the Constitution by creating spending. The government is taking the law to the Tribunal Constitucional, Peru’s constitutional court, and the Colegio de Economistas is doing the same separately. Meanwhile, Congress faces scrutiny over a 15% pay rise for its workers.

Peru’s Congress in Lima. The finance ministry says Congress cannot create spending. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

Minister calls pension law illegal

Peru’s finance minister, Elmer Cuba, says the teacher pension law is illegal. He says it puts macroeconomic stability at risk.

The law, Ley No. 32581, sets pensions for retired and former teachers. It ties the pension to the first magisterial scale, currently S/3,500.70 (about US$1,041).

Cuba argues Congress overstepped its constitutional role. He said: ‘Here the Constitution has been violated.

What is illegal is that congresses have a spending initiative.’

He also said the law puts the country’s macroeconomic stability at risk. The minister warned that no government can comply with what Congress approved without proper funding.

The law was promulgated in April 2026 but still has no implementing regulations. The reglamento deadline was 90 days from the law taking effect and expired around 16 July 2026.

The Senate has formally demanded that the finance ministry issue the regulations. But the ministry is focused on challenging the law instead.

Cuba says the government will take the law to the Tribunal Constitucional, Peru’s constitutional court. The Colegio de Economistas is doing the same separately.

The cost is high: the Consejo Fiscal, the independent fiscal watchdog, puts it at at least S/8,000 million a year. That is about US$2,378 million.

The Executive will also try to negotiate a smaller pension increase with teachers’ groups. This is a parallel path to the court challenge.

Cuba says the MEF is open to a pension hike, but not the one set by the law. The government wants to find a fiscally responsible figure.

The law remains on the books but without regulations, so it is not being applied. This creates a vacuum that the court will eventually fill.

Until then, teachers wait, and the government prepares its legal defense. The Tribunal Constitucional’s decision will be final.

If the law is struck down, the government avoids a major fiscal burden. If it stands, Peru must find the funds or cut elsewhere.

Cuba’s stance is clear: the practice is unconstitutional. His comments have set the stage for a legal battle over the pension’s fate.

Government plans to block the law

Congress workers get 15% pay rise

A separate collective agreement raised salaries for all Congress staff by 15%. It was signed under Fernando Rospigliosi’s Mesa Directiva.

The agreement was signed on 24 November 2025. The raise started on 1 January 2026 and lasts until December 2027.

It covers workers under the Sitracon union. Fernando Rospigliosi, then Congress president, signed the deal.

TV program ‘Punto Final’ revealed the increase on 16 August 2026. Reports say he tried to keep it secret.

The raise covers ‘all workers of the Parliament’ per media. Its exact scope is limited to the bargaining unit.

Union leaders who signed include Tulio Vizcarra Basto, Jorge Pacheco Munayco, Percy Ayala Ávila, Jaime Montoya Luna, Julio Barrera Egoavil, and Carlos Negrete Venegas. The pay rise stayed quiet until the TV report.

This raises questions about fiscal discipline. Lawmakers approve spending for themselves and staff, but challenge teacher pension increases.

For those in or invested in Latin America, this is a fiscal discipline story. Peru’s government fights a law that would add public spending.

A court challenge could set a precedent for similar pension demands elsewhere. The Congress pay rise shows how political and union pressures shape spending.

This matters for watchers of fiscal discipline across the region. Brazil, Argentina, and others face similar public sector wage battles.

Investors in Peruvian bonds or stocks should watch the Tribunal Constitucional’s decision. If the law stands, Peru may need more funds or cut elsewhere.

That could affect the budget deficit and the sol. The exchange rate is about 3.3647 soles per US dollar.

So the pension is roughly US$1,041 a month. That is a big cost for the treasury.

The outcome will show how committed the government is to controlling spending.

Why this matters for Latin America

Next steps and outlook

The government will take legal action soon. It also plans to talk with teacher unions about a smaller pension increase.

The Tribunal Constitucional, Peru’s top court, will decide if the law is legal. This could take months.

Until then, the law exists but has no rules. So it is not being used yet.

People should watch for any money effects and the court’s decision. The result will shape Peru’s pension and budget plans.

The minister says clearly: no spending that breaks the law. But political pressure is strong.

Teachers and unions will not give up easily. The government must balance legal rules with social needs.

Wait for the court’s ruling. It will be a big decision for Peru’s financial future.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Peru’s finance minister in August 2026? Elmer Cuba is the Minister of Economy and Finance, confirmed in multiple August 2026 reports. What does Ley No. 32581 do? It sets a pension floor for retired teachers equal to S/3,500.70 (about US$1,041), tied to the first magisterial scale. Why does Cuba call the pension law illegal? He says the practice of Congress initiating spending is illegal under Peru’s Constitution. That power belongs to the Executive. How did Congress workers get a 15% raise? A collective agreement signed on 24 November 2025 under Fernando Rospigliosi, then president of Congress. It took effect 1 January 2026.

Molinos Agro holds 65% of the project, and ACA holds 35%. ACA is the Asociacion de Cooperativas Argentinas, a farm cooperative group. Location The plant will be built in Timbues, Santa Fe, a key grain port area on the Parana River.

The project costs more than US$500 million. That is a large bet on Argentina’s soybean future. Capacity The plant will crush 15,000 tons of soybeans per day. That works out to about 5 million tons per year.

The plant will crush 15,000 tons of soybeans per day. That works out to about 5 million tons per year. Construction Building is expected to take about three years.

Building is expected to take about three years. Taxes The investment relies on planned cuts to export taxes, called retenciones or DEX, starting January 2027.

A US$500 million plant in Timbues is the first big new soy crushing investment in twelve years, betting on Argentina’s export tax cuts starting January 2027.

Molinos Agro and ACA are building a US$500 million soybean crushing plant in Timbues, Santa Fe. The project was announced on 8 July 2026, and it is the first major new soy crushing investment in twelve years. What has changed since is the tax schedule that makes it work, with export tax cuts starting January 2027.

Grain shipping on the Parana. The new Timbues plant will crush 15,000 tonnes of soybeans a day. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

A big bet on Argentine soybeans

Molinos Agro and ACA are putting more than US$500 million into a new soybean crushing plant in Timbues, Santa Fe. Timbues is on the Parana River, a key route for shipping grain.

Molinos Agro will own 65% of the project. ACA, a group of Argentine farm cooperatives, will own the other 35%.

The plant will crush 15,000 tons of soybeans each day. That is about 5 million tons a year, which would make it one of the biggest crush plants in the country.

This is the first major new soy crushing investment in twelve years. It was announced on 8 July 2026, and building will take about three years.

The plant will turn soybeans into meal and oil for world markets inside Argentina. This adds value at home instead of shipping raw beans.

Why export taxes matter here

The project needs a planned cut in export taxes, called retenciones or DEX. The Argentine government will reduce these taxes slowly, starting in January 2027.

Under this plan, soybean export taxes drop from 24% to 21% by the end of 2027. By December 2028, they would go down further to 15%.

Lower export taxes make it cheaper to sell soybean products abroad. That helps profits for a new crush plant, so the investment depends on this tax schedule.

The gap between soy and maize export taxes matters. Consultant Javier Preciado Patino, writing on 14 August 2026, says it is 15.5 points now.

It will fall to 13.5 points in 2027. By late 2028, it will be about 9.5 points.

The Bolsa de Comercio de Rosario, an exchange in the grain city of Rosario, tracks total tax payments. It says the six main agricultural chains will pay US$4,613 million in export taxes in 2026.

That is down from US$4,665 million in 2025, a fall of about 1%.

For 2026, the breakdown is: soybeans US$3,275 million, maize US$754 million, wheat US$324 million, sunflower US$158 million, barley US$79 million, and sorghum US$22 million.

The plant will cost more than US$500 million. That is a large capital outlay for Argentina’s agribusiness sector.

What the tax schedule means for the plant

The plant was announced in July 2026, but the tax changes are new. The schedule makes the project work by improving profit margins over the next few years.

As soybean export taxes drop, it becomes more attractive to crush beans in Argentina. The soy-versus-maize gap is key because it affects which crops farmers plant and how much they process.

The tax plan is not a signed decree yet. It depends on future policy decisions and could change.

If the schedule slips, the plant’s economics could change too. Watch the January 2027 start date, because that is when the bet starts to pay off.

The numbers behind the investment

The plant will crush 15,000 tons of soybeans each day, or about 5 million tons per year. That makes it one of the biggest crushing plants in the country.

This project is a bet on policy, not just on production. It expects Argentina to keep more soybeans at home for processing, instead of sending them out raw.

US Department of Agriculture forecasts for Argentina have not changed. The investment is based on local policy shifts, not US reports.

Why this matters for Latin America investors

For people invested in Argentine farming, this plant shows trust in the country’s export future. It also shows how tax cuts and other policy changes can push large investments.

Soybeans bring in billions of dollars in export income every year. A new crushing plant could change where value is added, keeping more of it in Argentina.

Workers and local suppliers in Santa Fe may gain new jobs and demand. Ports near Timbues will likely handle more soybean meal and oil exports.

This is the first big soy crushing investment in twelve years. That marks a renewed sense of confidence in Argentine soybeans.

Frequently Asked Questions

The investment is more than US$500 million. The plant will crush 15,000 tons of soybeans per day, about 5 million tons per year. When was the plant announced? The plant was announced on 8 July 2026. It is the first major new soy crushing investment in twelve years. Why is the plant linked to export taxes? Argentina plans to gradually reduce export taxes, called retenciones or DEX, starting January 2027. The soy export tax falls from 24% to 21% by the end of 2027 and to 15% by December 2028. Is the export tax cut guaranteed? No. It is a government schedule and not a signed decree. The plan could change.

Cuneo family sells 1% block

The Cuneo family sold 25 million Falabella shares on 13 August 2026. That is 1% of the retail company.

Bethia, tied to the Heller Solari family, sold two tranches. The first was 12.5 million shares for CLP 79,375 million on 20 January.

The second was 12.5 million shares for CLP 81,375 million on 23 January.

Paola Cuneo sold through Inversiones Santa Victoria SpA. Giorgianna Cuneo sold through Inversiones Cinque Terre SpA.

Each sold 12.5 million shares at an average price of CLP 6,300.20 each. The total value was CLP 157,504 million, about US$172.7 million.

The broker LarrainVial executed the block trade at about 10:30. After the sale, the Cuneo family’s combined holding fell to 8.24%, down from about 9.24%.

Founding families reduce stakes through 2026

The Cuneo sale is part of a wider trend. The founding families have sold 2.49% of Falabella in 2026.

These sales total CLP 401,549 million, about US$439 million, based on filings with Chile’s securities regulator, the CMF.

Mis Inversiones SpA, linked to the Del Rio Goudie family, sold 10 million shares, 0.39%, for CLP 65,100 million on 23 January. DT D y D, linked to Juan Pablo del Rio, sold 3 million shares, 0.12%, for CLP 18,195 million on 19 June.

LarrainVial pauses fund contributions

On 17 August 2026, LarrainVial’s LV Enfoque fund stopped new contributions for a while. The fund had about US$640 million at the end of July.

The manager wants to check if market liquidity levels will stay. Redemptions still work, and there are exceptions for planned savings plans and dividend reinvestment.

This is about the fund’s size and market liquidity, not a problem with the Santiago exchange.

Mallplaza revives Concón project

Separately, Mallplaza restarted a long-paused mall project in Concón. It shared the new design on 17 August 2026.

The project will be an open-air lifestyle centre at Bosques de Montemar. It will cost about US$80 million and have 50,000 square metres of leasable space, with around 200 shops.

The 2012 plan was 60,000 square metres and US$120 million, but it was dropped in 2024. The land has been involved since a purchase in 2011.

Mallplaza has talked with local residents and authorities about the new plan. Building is expected to finish around 2030.

Why this matters for investors

If you own Falabella shares, watch how they are sold. When founding families reduce their shares, it often means they see limited future gains.

The stock closed at CLP 6,180 on 14 August, the last close before Monday. That is the key price point to watch.

For those invested in Chilean retail, the Concón project is positive. It shows Mallplaza is willing to invest in growth after years of delay.

LarrainVial’s role as broker is notable. It handles major block trades, and its fund pause reflects a cautious stance on liquidity.

Who else has been selling

The Cuneo block was not the first sale this year. Bethia, the vehicle of the Heller Solari family, sold two tranches in January.

The first was 12,500,000 shares for CLP$79,375 million (about US$87 million) on 20 January. The second was another 12,500,000 shares for CLP$81,375 million (about US$89 million) on 23 January.

On the same day in January, Mis Inversiones SpA, linked to Del Rio Goudie, sold 10,000,000 shares — 0.39% of the company — for CLP$65,100 million (about US$71 million).

DT D y D, linked to Juan Pablo del Rio, followed in June with 3,000,000 shares, or 0.12%, for CLP$18,195 million (about US$20 million).

What Mallplaza is actually reviving

The Concon project has a long history. Mallplaza bought the land in 2011 and drew up a plan in 2012 for 60,000 square metres at a cost of about US$120 million.

That version was dropped in 2024. What returns now is smaller and open-air.

The new plan is about US$80 million for 50,000 square metres of leasable space and around 200 shops at Bosques de Montemar. It is due to open in 2030.

How much did the Cuneo family receive from the sale? They received CLP 157,504 million, about US$172.7 million. The average price was CLP 6,300.20 per share. How much of Falabella have the founding families sold in 2026? They sold 2.49% of the company in 2026. This raised about CLP 401,549 million, or US$439 million. World.content:
Colombia · Government

Key Facts Contracts More than 1,051 contracts were signed in the current budget year under the public media system.

More than 1,051 contracts were signed in the current budget year under the public media system. Value The combined value exceeds COP 100,000 million (about US$32 million at current exchange rates).

The combined value exceeds COP 100,000 million (about US$32 million at current exchange rates). Recent Between 6 and 7 August 2026, officials signed 87 contracts worth about COP 4,000 million (about US$1.3 million).

All these contracts will be reviewed as part of a reorganisation announced by the new management of Inravision. Entity Inravision, the public broadcaster formerly known as RTVC, manages the Sistema de Medios Publicos de Colombia.

Inravision, the public broadcaster formerly known as RTVC, manages the Sistema de Medios Publicos de Colombia. Context President Abelardo De la Espriella’s government has moved to restructure public institutions since taking office.

New management of Colombia’s public media system will review more than 1,051 contracts worth over COP 100,000 million (about US$32 million).

Colombia’s new public media management will review more than 1,051 contracts signed this year. The total value exceeds COP 100,000 million (about US$32 million). The review is part of a broader push for transparency under President Abelardo de la Espriella, who took office on 7 August 2026. For anyone who does business with the state, this is a signal: contracts signed under the previous government are now under the microscope.

The Palacio de San Carlos in Bogota. The foreign ministry is investigating its ambassador to Haiti. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What the contract review covers

On 17 August 2026, a MinTIC statement following an extraordinary board meeting on 15 August disclosed the contract numbers. The statement came from the new administration of the Sistema de Medios Publicos de Colombia, which operates as Inravision, the public broadcaster formerly known as RTVC.

The statement said the contracts were signed in the current budget year. The total value is more than COP 100,000 million, which equals about US$32 million.

Between 6 and 7 August 2026, 87 contracts were signed for approximately COP 4,000 million. That is about US$1.3 million.

All of these processes will be subject to review as part of the reorganisation announced by the new management of Inravision. The review aims to check how the contracts were awarded.

The reorganisation began on 7 August, right after the news programming strand, the franja informativa, ended on 6 August.

Understanding the institutional names

The organisation formerly called RTVC Sistema de Medios Publicos is now Inravision Sistema de Medios Publicos. RTVC announced in April 2026 that it was taking back its historic name.

Write it as ‘Inravision, the public broadcaster formerly known as RTVC’.

The new gerente — general manager — is Angela Maria Mora Soto, a lawyer appointed by the government of Abelardo De la Espriella. She replaces Hollman Morris.

The ICT minister is Alexandra Falla.

Do not assume these 1,051 contracts belong solely to RTVC. The reporting groups them under the public media system umbrella.

This difference matters for investors and professionals who follow government contracts. The legal entity in charge of each contract can change.

Why the review matters now

President Abelardo De la Espriella took office on 7 August 2026.

The contract review is part of a wider reorganisation of public media. This may lead to new buying rules or the ending of some contracts.

For businesses that work with public broadcasters, this review creates uncertainty. Existing contracts may be delayed or renegotiated.

The review also shows how the new administration wants to spend public money. They will look closely at contracts signed by the previous government.

What happens next

The new management has not said when the review will finish. They have said all processes will be checked during the restructuring.

No contracts have been cancelled or suspended so far. The review is still in its early stages.

Watch for news from Inravision about findings or changes. The government may also release new rules for contracts.

For now, this is a review, not a cancellation. Contract holders should watch for updates and keep their documents ready.

This review is part of a larger effort by the De la Espriella government to change state agencies. The pension reform and diplomatic appointments are also being looked at.

Vilma Velasquez, Colombia’s ambassador to Haiti, is under investigation by the foreign ministry. The issue is about US$500,000 in unexplained transfers, including a cheque from the embassy’s operating account to her personal account.

This was reported on 7 August 2026. She denies the claim, saying 500,000 dollars never came in.

She was already suspended by the Procuraduria in May 2026 for backing Ivan Cepeda in politics.

The Constitutional Court may send the pension reform back to Congress again. This would be the second time.

The plans for savers and for moving funds to Colpensiones are still being discussed.

The total amount is about COP 25 billones, which is close to 25 trillion Colombian pesos. That is about US$8 billion.

These actions share a common idea: the new government is taking more control over institutions and contracts. Investors should expect more reviews and possible changes in policy.

Broader context for investors

Vilma Velasquez, Colombia’s ambassador to Haiti, is under investigation by the foreign ministry over about US$500,000 in unjustified transfers, including a cheque from the embassy’s operating account to her personal account. This came out on 7 August 2026. She denies it, saying 500,000 dollars never came in. She had already been suspended by the Procuraduria in May 2026 for political participation, for backing Ivan Cepeda.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many contracts are under review? More than 1,051 contracts signed in the current budget year are under review. They belong to the public media system managed by Inravision. What is the total value of the contracts? The total value exceeds COP 100,000 million, which is about US$32 million. An additional 87 contracts signed in early August are worth about COP 4,000 million (US$1.3 million). Are these contracts being cancelled? No. They are under review as part of a reorganisation. No cancellations have been announced so far. Which entity signed these contracts? The reporting refers to the Sistema de Medios Publicos de Colombia and Inravision, the public broadcaster formerly known as RTVC. The figures cover the public media system.

World.title: A Week On, Colombia’s Quake Toll Is Still Moving
World.content:
Colombia · Disaster

Key Facts The toll As of the national disaster agency’s 16 August evening cut, 287 people are dead. Also, 4,147 are injured, 194 are still missing, and 355 were rescued.

As of the national disaster agency’s 16 August evening cut, 287 people are dead. Also, 4,147 are injured, 194 are still missing, and 355 were rescued. The damage The disaster destroyed 26,392 homes and damaged 127,608 more. In total, 197 buildings collapsed across 472 municipalities in 15 departments.

The disaster destroyed 26,392 homes and damaged 127,608 more. In total, 197 buildings collapsed across 472 municipalities in 15 departments. The reach The event affected 185,996 people and 120,671 families. It also hit 3,207 schools, 304 health centres, and 410 roads.

The event affected 185,996 people and 120,671 families. It also hit 3,207 schools, 304 health centres, and 410 roads. Numbers move both ways The count was 294 on 15 August and 287 on 16 August. Falling tolls are normal in the first fortnight, because duplicates get removed as names are confirmed.

The count was 294 on 15 August and 287 on 16 August. Falling tolls are normal in the first fortnight, because duplicates get removed as names are confirmed. A private cheque David Vélez, the Colombian co-founder and chief executive of Nubank, is giving COP$100,000 million, which is about US$32 million, towards reconstruction.

David Vélez, the Colombian co-founder and chief executive of Nubank, is giving COP$100,000 million, which is about US$32 million, towards reconstruction. The politics A censure motion against Housing Minister Jaime Andrés Beltrán was announced on 17 August. This happened because of photographs of him on the beach in Santa Marta during the emergency.

Seven days after a magnitude 7.4 quake hit Chocó, the official count is still being revised in both directions — and the politics has arrived.

If you have been trying to follow Colombia’s earthquake from abroad, the hardest part is that the numbers keep changing. A week after the magnitude 7.4 quake struck on 10 August, centred five kilometres south of San José del Palmar in Chocó, the official toll has gone up and then back down. Here is where it actually stood at the last full count, and what has happened around it since.

President Abelardo De la Espriella announced the Nubank founder’s donation. A censure motion against the housing minister followed. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

Where the count stands

The national disaster agency, UNGRD, gives updates from time to time, not live numbers. Its last full count, at 18:30 on 16 August, showed 287 dead and 4,147 injured.

Another 194 people are still missing. Also, 355 have been pulled out alive.

Watch these two numbers because the gap between them shows where the toll will change next. The damage is huge for a country this size.

26,392 homes were destroyed. 127,608 were damaged, and 197 buildings fell.

Damage hit 472 municipalities across 15 departments. Public buildings also suffered: 3,207 schools, 304 health centres, and 410 roads were affected.

On 15 August, the official figure was 294. On 16 August, it was 287.

A falling toll can look scary if you have not seen it before, so here is why. In the first days after a disaster, the same person may be counted more than once.

For example, one count may come from a town, another from a hospital, and another from a rescue team. As names get confirmed, duplicate counts are removed.

For anyone watching from far away, write down the time and date for every number you see. A figure without a date is not very useful this week.

This is the mistake most news reports make. On 12 August, the governor of Chocó, Nubia Carolina Córdoba-Curi, said the search and rescue phase was over in her area.

She said they were no longer looking for people under the rubble.

Why the death toll went down

The search is over in Chocó, not nationally

That rule applies only to Chocó. The national emergency is still active, because 194 people remain missing.

So reports that Colombia has stopped searching are only partly correct. Chocó has moved to rebuilding, but other areas have not.

Money, tolls and a minister at the beach

David Vélez, founder and leader of Nubank, is giving COP$100,000 million — about US$32 million — for reconstruction. He confirmed this himself after President Abelardo de la Espriella announced it.

The road agency ANI, led by president Ricardo Ayerbe, has removed tolls, but less widely than news suggests. The waiver covers trucks with heavy machines, emergency gear, and aid supplies, on specific roads only.

Those roads are Buga–Buenaventura, Malla Vial del Valle, Armenia–Pereira–Manizales, Tercer Carril Bogotá–Girardot, and Girardot–Ibagué–Cajamarca. Fines for overloaded trucks are paused, so aid vehicles are not penalised.

Private car drivers still pay.

Politics has entered too. On 17 August, a censure motion was announced against Housing Minister Jaime Andrés Beltrán, due to photos of him at a beach in Santa Marta during the emergency.

It is announced, but not yet voted on.

What this means if you live in or invest in the region

Housing will shape the coming two years. With 26,392 homes destroyed and 127,608 damaged, this becomes a rebuilding and money story long after rescue work ends.

The roads on ANI’s list are the same ones used for cargo between Buenaventura, Colombia’s main Pacific port, and the inland areas. Businesses moving goods through that port should check ANI notices, not general headlines.

The Vélez donation matters for another reason. US$32 million from one private person is a big part of the early rebuilding costs.

This amount sets a new level for other big Colombian companies to compare with.

The censure motion shows how fast disaster aid turns into politics in this country. If you have projects waiting for housing-ministry decisions, this is a delay risk you should plan for.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many people died in Colombia’s earthquake? The national disaster agency UNGRD recorded 287 deaths in its cut at 18:30 on 16 August 2026, with 4,147 injured and 194 people still missing. The figure moves between cuts, so always check the date attached to it. Why did the death toll go down? It was 294 on 15 August and 287 on 16 August. Early counts often double-record the same victim through different channels, and duplicates are removed as identities are confirmed. Has the search for survivors ended? In Chocó, yes — the governor declared the search and rescue phase over on 12 August. Nationally it remains open, with 194 people still unaccounted for. Are Colombia’s toll roads free after the earthquake? Only for specific vehicles. ANI has exempted vehicles carrying heavy machinery, emergency equipment and humanitarian aid on a defined list of corridors, and suspended overload fines. Private cars still pay.

World.title: Peru’s Mining Boom: Investment Up 42.7%, Not 74%
World.content:
Peru · Mining

Key Facts Investment rise Peru’s mining investment grew 42.7% year-on-year to US$3.304 billion in H1 2026, per MINEM and Andina.

Peru’s mining investment grew 42.7% year-on-year to US$3.304 billion in H1 2026, per MINEM and Andina. The 74% myth A widely shared figure of +74% is actually Fresnillo’s revenue increase (up 74.7% to US$3.38 billion), a Mexico-only company, not a Peru sector total.

A widely shared figure of +74% is actually Fresnillo’s revenue increase (up 74.7% to US$3.38 billion), a Mexico-only company, not a Peru sector total. Top spenders Leading investors include Southern Peru (US$432.7 million, up 101.1%), Shougang Hierro Peru (US$314.4 million, up 135.4%), Las Bambas (US$275.5 million, up 50.5%), Antamina (US$271.6 million, up 31.2%), Buenaventura (US$174.2 million, up 2.4%), and Cerro Verde (US$169.3 million, up 3.8%).

Leading investors include Southern Peru (US$432.7 million, up 101.1%), Shougang Hierro Peru (US$314.4 million, up 135.4%), Las Bambas (US$275.5 million, up 50.5%), Antamina (US$271.6 million, up 31.2%), Buenaventura (US$174.2 million, up 2.4%), and Cerro Verde (US$169.3 million, up 3.8%). Company profits MMG (which runs Las Bambas in Peru) reported profit after tax of US$1,366.0 million, up 89%—not 141%, which is the rise in cash.

MMG (which runs Las Bambas in Peru) reported profit after tax of US$1,366.0 million, up 89%—not 141%, which is the rise in cash. Quellaveco shines Anglo American’s Quellaveco mine brought in US$2.161 billion in revenue, up from US$1.524 billion a year earlier.

Anglo American’s Quellaveco mine brought in US$2.161 billion in revenue, up from US$1.524 billion a year earlier. Copper giant Southern Copper’s first-half net sales were US$8.54 billion, up 38.4% (US$8,540.4m against US$6,172.9m).

Southern Copper’s first-half net sales were US$8.54 billion, up 38.4% (US$8,540.4m against US$6,172.9m). Weak spot Exploration spending rose only 1.3%, to US$336.4 million, even as investment boomed.

The real story: Peru’s mining investment hit US$3.3 billion in H1 2026, up 42.7% year-on-year. That 74% figure? It’s a Mexican miner’s revenue.

If you’ve seen headlines about Peru’s mining sector surging 74%, you might be forgiven for thinking the country is swimming in cash. But the actual official figure is different: mining investment rose 42.7% to US$3.304 billion in the first half of 2026, according to Peru’s Ministry of Energy and Mines (MINEM) via state news agency Andina. The 74% bump belongs to Fresnillo, a Mexico-only miner—not Peru. Let’s clear up the confusion so you know what’s really happening on the ground.

An open-pit operation in the Peruvian Andes. Mining investment reached US$3.304 billion in the first half of 2026. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

The real numbers from MINEM

Peru’s Ministry of Energy and Mines (MINEM) says mining investment reached US$3.304 billion in the first half of 2026. That is 42.7% more than the US$2.3152 billion from the same time last year.

This is the official total for the whole mining sector. It shows steady growth, but not the 74% jump that some headlines mention.

MINEM lists the top investors as Southern Peru, Shougang Hierro Peru, Las Bambas, Antamina, Buenaventura, and Cerro Verde. Southern Peru alone spent US$432.7 million, which is 101.1% above a year ago.

Exploration spending is the weak part. It rose only 1.3%, reaching US$336.4 million.

Investment is strong, but finding new mineral deposits is slow. For comparison, US$3.304 billion equals about 11.1 billion soles, using the rate of 3.3647 soles per US dollar.

This healthy number shows mining firms are confident and spending on projects. That is important because Peru is the world’s second-largest copper producer.

The 74% figure is real, but it does not apply to Peru. It comes from Fresnillo, a mining company based in Mexico, whose first-half 2026 revenue rose 74.7% to US$3.38 billion.

Fresnillo also reported a net profit of US$1.46 billion, up 213%. But it has no mines in Peru—its operations are at Saucito, Herradura, Juanicipio, Fresnillo, Cienega, and San Julian.

That 74% figure does not reflect Peru’s mining health. If you see such claims, check the source carefully.

Anglo American’s Quellaveco mine in Peru earned US$2.161 billion in revenue. That is up from US$1.524 billion in H1 2025, a 41.8% increase.

Higher copper prices and output helped the rise. Production was slightly lower, but the result still improved.

The official Peruvian number is the 42.7% investment rise. Trust that one instead.

Why does this matter? Investment shows what companies plan for the future.

Profits can change quickly, but spending signals long-term confidence.

The confusion likely comes from mixing company results with sector data. For example, MMG’s profit jumped, but that is just one firm, not all miners.

Fresnillo’s revenue growth is big, but it belongs to a different country. Peru-linked miners still had a strong first half, even if the 74% headline is wrong.

MMG, which runs the Las Bambas copper mine in Peru, reported profit after tax of US$1,366.0 million, up 89%. Profit for equity holders was US$897.2 million.

Some say 141% growth, but that number is for cash, not earnings. Las Bambas drove the result, and MMG called it its best financial performance in over ten years.

Southern Copper, which operates major mines in Peru, posted first-half net sales of US$8.54 billion, up 38.4%. Its second quarter alone brought in US$4,289.0 million.

Where the 74% figure really comes from

Company-level wins that tell the real story

Anglo American’s Quellaveco mine in Peru generated US$2.161 billion in revenue, up from US$1.524 billion in H1 2025. That’s a 41.8% increase, driven by higher copper prices and production—even though output was slightly lower. Southern Copper, which runs major mines in Peru, posted first-half net sales of US$8.54 billion, up 38.4%; the second quarter alone was US$4,289.0 million.

Buenaventura, a Peruvian miner, saw net income attributable of US$514.0 million on H1 revenue of US$1,153.6 million, both clearly higher than the same period in 2025. Nexa Resources’ Peru subsidiary, Nexa Resources Peru S.A.A., reported US$669 million in revenue, up 45%—not the group.

The Nexa group’s first-half revenue was US$1,796 million, up 34%.

Why this matters for you

If you’re invested in Latin America, these numbers matter because they show where capital is flowing. Peru is the world’s second-largest copper producer, and rising investment means more supply coming online—which could affect global copper prices and your portfolio.

For instance, MMG’s record profit and Southern Copper’s revenue surge are signals that copper demand remains strong.

For expats living in Peru, a mining boom often translates into more jobs, stronger local economies in mining regions, and a firmer sol. The currency has been stable, with the exchange rate around 3.36 soles per US dollar.

Mining investment also supports infrastructure and local businesses, from equipment suppliers to service providers.

But don’t get caught up in the hype. The 74% figure is a classic example of a number being taken out of context. Stick to the official MINEM data, and you’ll have a clearer picture of what’s actually happening. And if you’re watching specific stocks, remember that company-level results can vary widely—so look at each miner’s own numbers, not just the sector headline. Also, note that Peru’s energy and mines minister is Guillermo Shinno Huamani, sworn in in late July 2026 under President Keiko Fujimori—his office is the source for the official investment data.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the official figure for Peru’s mining investment in H1 2026? Peru’s Ministry of Energy and Mines (MINEM) reported mining investment of US$3.304 billion in the first half of 2026, up 42.7% year-on-year. Where does the 74% figure come from? The 74% figure is actually Fresnillo’s revenue growth—up 74.7% to US$3.38 billion. Fresnillo is a Mexico-only miner, not a Peru-specific metric. Which companies led mining investment in Peru? According to MINEM, the top investors include Southern Peru (US$432.7 million, up 101.1%), Shougang Hierro Peru (US$314.4 million, up 135.4%), Las Bambas (US$275.5 million, up 50.5%), Antamina (US$271.6 million, up 31.2%), Buenaventura (US$174.2 million, up 2.4%), and Cerro Verde (US$169.3 million, up 3.8%). How did Peru-linked miners perform in H1 2026? MMG’s Las Bambas contributed to a US$1,366.0 million profit after tax, up 89%. Anglo American’s Quellaveco saw US$2.161 billion in revenue. Southern Copper reported first-half net sales of US$8.54 billion, up 38.4%.

World.title: Mexico’s Military Service Draw: Who the 2026 Lottery Covers
World.content:
Mexico · Explainer

Key Facts Lottery date: The Servicio Militar Nacional (SMN) draft lottery for Clase 2008 — men turning 18 in 2026 — is set for November 2026, according to SEDENA official information. The exact day hasn’t been published.

The Servicio Militar Nacional (SMN) draft lottery for Clase 2008 — men turning 18 in 2026 — is set for November 2026, according to SEDENA official information. The exact day hasn’t been published. Who is drawn: The main class is men born in 2008, turning 18 this year, plus ‘remisos’ — men who missed registering when they should have. The November draw assigns a white or blue ball for ‘encuadrado’ (you serve) or a black ball for ‘disponibilidad’ (standby).

The November draft lottery has a clear target group — and it isn’t everyone aged 18 to 39.

If you’ve seen posts claiming Mexico is about to draft everyone aged 18 to 39 into the Army, take a breath. Nothing changed this month. The claim doing the rounds is recycled coverage of SEDENA’s January 2026 convocatoria — the routine annual cycle being reported as news.

Mexico’s military service draw is held in November. No new rule was announced in August. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What the lottery actually is

SMN is Mexico’s required military service. Under the Ley del Servicio Militar, ‘service of arms’ is a duty for Mexican citizens by birth or naturalization.

The lottery decides if men are ‘encuadrado’ — meaning they must train. Or they are ‘disponibilidad’ (standby).

For 2026, the group is ‘Clase 2008’ — men born in 2008 who turn 18 this year. SEDENA (Mexico’s defense ministry) said the lottery for this group will be in November 2026.

Those picked for encuadrado attend 13 Saturday sessions starting in 2027.

The 18-to-39 age number online is true, but it doesn’t mean what viral posts suggest. It refers to ‘remisos’ — men who missed their SMN paperwork on time.

These men still must fix their status. A remiso must regularize their status to get their military card.

They remain obligated until December 31 of the year they turn 40. So the age range can be 18 to 39.

The law was first published in 1940. Its latest update was on May 18, 2022.

The process has five steps: registration (alistamiento), lottery (sorteo), recruitment (reclutamiento), training (adiestramiento), and freeing your military card (liberación).

So the 18-to-39 window is about fixing missed paperwork, not a new draft for all up to middle age. The main group is still men turning 18 in 2026.

For Mexican men, the SMN is an ‘obligación ineludible’ (unavoidable duty), per SEDENA communications. If you’re a man turning 18 in 2026, registration is a legal duty, not a choice.

If chosen encuadrado, attending the 13 Saturday sessions is required. Missing them could mean legal trouble, with up to one year in prison as the law mentions.

The 18-to-39 age range, explained

What’s compulsory, and for whom

For women, the rules are different. Participation in the SMN is strictly voluntary, and they are not subject to encuadramiento.

This has been the case since 2000.

What’s actually new for 2026

The basic structure of the SMN hasn’t changed. There’s no new SEDENA notice and nothing in the official gazette for August 2026.

The claim doing the rounds is the routine annual cycle being reported as news.

The 2026 convocatoria, which dates to January, opens the municipal registration window from 2 January to 15 October 2026. The Ley del Servicio Militar sets preliminaries for the second half of the year a man turns 18.

This is the same annual process. The November draw assigns a white or blue ball for ‘encuadrado’ — meaning you serve — and a black ball for ‘disponibilidad’.

Cartilla liberation is in December 2026.

Why this matters for you

If you’re a Mexican man who never completed your SMN paperwork, the clock is ticking. The remiso window is real, and the November 2026 lottery for Clase 2008 is the one that applies to you most directly if you’re in that class.

But even if you’re older, you still need to regularize to get your cartilla before turning 40.

For expats and investors, the practical takeaway is simpler: there’s no mass mobilization coming. The SMN is a long-standing administrative process, and the 18-to-39 scare is a misreading of the remiso rule.

Your neighbor with a desk job isn’t about to be drafted.

If you have employees or family members facing this, the real deadline is paper-based: register, get your cartilla, and you’re done. The lottery is a formality for most.

Nothing in the sources suggests a shift that would affect labor markets, investment, or day-to-day life beyond the usual paperwork. The only people who need to act are those who’ve fallen behind on their SMN obligations — and they should treat this as a reminder to catch up.

No. The 18-to-39 range refers to ’remisos’ — men who missed registering for the SMN when they were due and must regularize their status to get their cartilla. The main conscription class for 2026 is men born in 2008, turning 18 this year. Claims about a mass draft of everyone up to 39 go beyond what the law and SEDENA state. When is the 2026 military service lottery? For Clase 2008, SEDENA officially informed that the lottery will be held in November 2026. The exact day hasn’t been published. Is military service compulsory for women in Mexico? No. Women’s participation in the SMN is strictly voluntary, and they are not subject to encuadramiento. This has been the case since 2000. What happens if I miss the registration deadline? You become a ’remiso’ — a man who didn’t complete SMN paperwork when due. You must regularize your status to obtain your cartilla, and you remain under obligation until December 31 of the year you turn 40. Legal consequences, including up to one year of prison by court order, are referenced under the law, though sources don’t clarify if this is newly enforced.
